claim: Surface proteins of Staphylococcus aureus are secreted across septal membranes for assembly into the bacterial cross-wall.
source: Surface proteins of Staphylococcus aureus are secreted across septal membranes for assembly into the bacterial cross-wall.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Localized secretion at septal membranes requires the YSIRK/GXXS motif signal peptide.
source: This localized secretion requires the YSIRK/GXXS motif signal peptide, however the mechanisms supporting precursor trafficking are not known.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature cited in the introduction.

claim: The signal peptide of staphylococcal protein A (SpA) is cleaved at the YSIRK/GXXS motif.
source: We show here that the signal peptide of staphylococcal protein A (SpA) is cleaved at the YSIRK/GXXS motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Edman degradation and mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: A SpA signal peptide mutant defective for YSIRK/GXXS cleavage is impaired for septal secretion.
source: A SpA signal peptide mutant defective for YSIRK/GXXS cleavage is also impaired for septal secretion and co-purifies with SecA, SecDF and LtaS.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1, 2, and 4 showing that SpA S18L mutant accumulates precursor and exhibits reduced septal secretion.

claim: SpA signal peptide mutant defective for YSIRK/GXXS cleavage co-purifies with SecA, SecDF and LtaS.
source: A SpA signal peptide mutant defective for YSIRK/GXXS cleavage is also impaired for septal secretion and co-purifies with SecA, SecDF and LtaS.
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking and affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: SecA depletion blocks precursor targeting to septal membranes.
source: SecA depletion blocks precursor targeting to septal membranes, whereas deletion of secDF diminishes SpA secretion into the cross-wall.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figures 6 and 8 showing that SpA precursors fail to localize to septal membranes when SecA is depleted.

claim: Deletion of secDF diminishes SpA secretion into the cross-wall.
source: SecA depletion blocks precursor targeting to septal membranes, whereas deletion of secDF diminishes SpA secretion into the cross-wall.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and microscopy data in Figure 9 showing reduced SpA secretion and cross-wall localization in secDF mutants.

claim: Depletion of LtaS blocks lipoteichoic acid synthesis.
source: Depletion of LtaS blocks lipoteichoic acid synthesis and abolishes SpA precursor trafficking to septal membranes.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature on LtaS function cited in the manuscript (Gründling and Schneewind, 2007).

claim: Depletion of LtaS abolishes SpA precursor trafficking to septal membranes.
source: Depletion of LtaS blocks lipoteichoic acid synthesis and abolishes SpA precursor trafficking to septal membranes.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 10 showing that SpA precursors mislocalize to polar membranes when LtaS is depleted.

claim: Surface proteins of S. aureus enter the secretory pathway with their N-terminal signal peptides.
source: Surface proteins of Staphylococcus aureus and other gram-positive cocci enter the secretory pathway with their N-terminal signal peptides (DeDent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Surface proteins are covalently linked to cell wall peptidoglycan via sortase A-catalyzed cleavage at the LPXTG motif.
source: Once translocated across the membrane, surface proteins are covalently linked to cell wall peptidoglycan via sortase A-catalyzed cleavage at the LPXTG motif of C-terminal sorting signals (Schneewind et al., 1992; Schneewind et al., 1995; Mazmanian et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Some surface proteins are secreted at septal membranes and incorporated into cross-wall peptidoglycan.
source: Some, but not all surface proteins are secreted at septal membranes and incorporated into cross-wall peptidoglycan (Cole and Hahn, 1962; Carlsson et al., 2006; DeDent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-wall anchored surface proteins are displayed over large segments of the bacterial surface following division and separation of daughter cells.
source: Following division and separation of spherical daughter cells, cross-wall anchored surface proteins are displayed over large segments of the bacterial surface (DeDent et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cross-wall trafficking of surface proteins requires a signal peptide with YSIRK/GXXS motif.
source: Cross-wall trafficking of surface proteins requires a signal peptide with YSIRK/GXXS motif (Carlsson et al., 2006; DeDent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The YSIRK/GXXS motif is positioned N-terminal of the hydrophobic core common to all signal peptide precursors traveling the Sec pathway.
source: The YSIRK/GXXS motif is positioned N-terminal of the hydrophobic core, common to all signal peptide precursors traveling the Sec pathway (Emr et al., 1978; Emr et al., 1981; von Heijne, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on signal peptide structure.

claim: Staphylococcal protein A (SpA) is synthesized as a precursor with an N-terminal YSIRK/GXXS signal peptide and a C-terminal LPXTG motif sorting signal.
source: SpA is synthesized as a precursor with an N-terminal YSIRK/GXXS signal peptide and a C-terminal LPXTG motif sorting signal (Abrahmsén et al., 1985; Schneewind et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SpA signal peptide is cleaved by signal peptidase after initiation into the secretion pathway.
source: After initiation into the secretion pathway, the signal peptide is cleaved by signal peptidase (Abrahmsén et al., 1985; Schallenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Newly synthesized SpA is secreted into the cross-wall compartment bounded by septal membranes of burgeoning cells during division.
source: Newly synthesized SpA is secreted into the cross-wall compartment, bounded by septal membranes of burgeoning cells during division (DeDent et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Staphylococci divide perpendicular to previous cell division planes.
source: Staphylococci divide perpendicular to previous cell division planes (Tzagoloff and Novick, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In S. aureus strain Newman, thirteen different sortase-anchored surface proteins and four additional proteins are endowed with YSIRK/GXXS signal peptides for septal secretion.
source: In S. aureus strain Newman, thirteen different sortase-anchored surface proteins and four additional proteins are endowed with YSIRK/GXXS signal peptides for septal secretion: lipase (Lip), glycerol-ester hydrolase (Geh), murein hydrolase LytN and the cell size determinant Ebh (Yu and Götz, 2012; Frankel et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SpAED was found in the extracellular medium and its precursor species was detected in the bacterial pellet.
source: SpAED was found in the extracellular medium; its precursor species was detected in the bacterial pellet (Figure 1bc).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Deletion of the YSIRK motif (ΔYSIRK) diminished the abundance of the SpAED/ΔYSIRK precursor and its processing.
source: Deletion of the YSIRK motif (ΔYSIRK) diminished the abundance of the SpAED/ΔYSIRK precursor and its processing (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Single amino acid substitutions at two positions in the YSIRK motif (I9S and R10A) resulted in precursor accumulation.
source: Single amino acid substitutions at two positions in the YSIRK motif (I9S and R10A) resulted in precursor accumulation (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The R10A variant exhibited diminished secretion and accumulated a precursor species that migrated faster on SDS-PAGE than the full-length precursor.
source: Further, the R10A variant exhibited diminished secretion and accumulated a precursor species that migrated faster on SDS-PAGE than the full-length precursor (Figure 1bc).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b and quantification in Figure 1c.

claim: Amino acid substitution at lysine 11 (K11A) of the YSIRK motif had no effect on SpAED/K11A precursor processing and secretion.
source: Amino acid substitution at lysine 11 (K11A) of the YSIRK motif had no effect on SpAED/K11A precursor processing and secretion (Figure 1bc).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b and quantification in Figure 1c.

claim: Deletion of GIAS (ΔGIAS) or of the two variable residues in the GXXS motif (ΔIA) caused precursor accumulation and blocked precursor processing.
source: Deletion of GIAS (ΔGIAS) or of the two variable residues in the GXXS motif (ΔIA) caused precursor accumulation and blocked precursor processing (Figure 1bc).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b and quantification in Figure 1c.

claim: Substitution of glycine 15 (G15L) reduced the abundance of SpAED/G15L and led to the accumulation of a unique precursor species that migrated faster on SDS-PAGE than full-length precursor.
source: Substitution of glycine 15 (G15L) reduced the abundance of SpAED/G15L and led to the accumulation of a unique precursor species that migrated faster on SDS-PAGE than full-length precursor (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Substitution of serine 18 (S18L) caused accumulation of full-length and processed precursors as well as reduced secretion.
source: Substitution of serine 18 (S18L) caused accumulation of full-length and processed precursors as well as reduced secretion (Figure 1bc).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1b and quantification in Figure 1c.

claim: The SpAED precursor was found in the cytoplasm and membrane, whereas mature product was secreted into the culture supernatant.
source: The SpAED precursor was found in the cytoplasm and membrane, whereas mature product was secreted into the culture supernatant (S) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Precursors of the SpAED/ΔIA and SpAED/R10A variants accumulated mostly in the cytoplasm.
source: Precursors of the SpAED/ΔIA and SpAED/R10A variants accumulated mostly in the cytoplasm, whereas the SpAED/S18L precursor was located predominantly in the membrane (Figure 2ab).
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2a and quantification in Figure 2b.

claim: The SpAED/S18L precursor was located predominantly in the membrane.
source: Precursors of the SpAED/ΔIA and SpAED/R10A variants accumulated mostly in the cytoplasm, whereas the SpAED/S18L precursor was located predominantly in the membrane (Figure 2ab).
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2a and quantification in Figure 2b.

claim: Wild-type SpAED precursor was processed within 60 s into mature, secreted product.
source: Pulse-labeling experiments revealed that wild-type SpAED precursor was processed within 60 s into mature, secreted product (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Processing of the SpAED/ΔIA, SpAED/R10A and SpAED/S18L precursors was delayed.
source: In contrast, processing of the SpAED/ΔIA, SpAED/R10A and SpAED/S18L precursors was delayed (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Wild-type SpA was assembled in the cross-wall compartment.
source: As expected, wild-type SpA was assembled in the cross-wall compartment, whereas SpASP-SasF, a protein A variant that is secreted via a canonical (non-YSIRK/GXXS) signal peptide, was deposited into peripheral segments of the cell wall envelope (DeDent et al., 2008)(Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: SpASP-SasF was deposited into peripheral segments of the cell wall envelope.
source: As expected, wild-type SpA was assembled in the cross-wall compartment, whereas SpASP-SasF, a protein A variant that is secreted via a canonical (non-YSIRK/GXXS) signal peptide, was deposited into peripheral segments of the cell wall envelope (DeDent et al., 2008)(Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2d and citation to prior work.

claim: SpAΔIA, SpAR10A and SpAS18L exhibited defects in surface display.
source: SpAΔIA, SpAR10A and SpAS18L exhibited defects in surface display, consistent with their observed defects in precursor processing and secretion (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Residual amounts of cross-wall localization were observed for SpAR10A and SpAS18L.
source: Residual amounts of cross-wall localization were observed for SpAR10A and SpAS18L, whereas SpAΔIA was not detected in the cross-wall compartment (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2e.

claim: SpAΔIA was not detected in the cross-wall compartment.
source: Residual amounts of cross-wall localization were observed for SpAR10A and SpAS18L, whereas SpAΔIA was not detected in the cross-wall compartment (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Edman degradation revealed that SpAED-2 is a product of proteolytic cleavage within the YSIRK/GXXS motif with N-terminus Gly13.
source: Edman degradation revealed that SpAED-2 is a product of proteolytic cleavage within the YSIRK/GXXS motif (N-terminus Gly13).
evidence: This is supported by Edman degradation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SpAED-3 is a product of further cleavage with N-terminal amino acid 10 residues downstream (N-terminus Thr23).
source: SpAED-3 is a product of further cleavage, as Edman degradation identified its N-terminal amino acid 10 residues downstream (N-terminus Thr23) (Figure 3ab).
evidence: This is supported by Edman degradation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MALDI-TOF-MS analysis confirmed the predicted mass of the SpAED precursor and its cleaved species.
source: Purified SpAED-1 precursor as well as its SpAED-2, SpAED-3 and SpAED-4 cleavage products were analyzed by MALDI-TOF-MS, confirming the predicted mass of the precursor and its cleaved species (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: The SpA precursor (SpAED-1) is cleaved between Leu12 and Gly13, which are positioned between the two motifs of the YSIRKL/GVGIAS sequence.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the SpA precursor (SpAED-1) is cleaved between Leu12 and Gly13, which are positioned between the two motifs (underlined) of the YSIRKL/GVGIAS sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from Edman degradation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The R10A substitution alters the cleavage site and diminishes precursor cleavage.
source: The R10A substitution alters the cleavage site and diminishes precursor cleavage, whereas the S18L substitution and ΔIA deletion diminish precursor cleavage without altering the cleavage site between the YSIRK/GXXS motifs.
evidence: This is inferred from Edman degradation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The S18L substitution and ΔIA deletion diminish precursor cleavage without altering the cleavage site between the YSIRK/GXXS motifs.
source: The R10A substitution alters the cleavage site and diminishes precursor cleavage, whereas the S18L substitution and ΔIA deletion diminish precursor cleavage without altering the cleavage site between the YSIRK/GXXS motifs.
evidence: This is inferred from Edman degradation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Precursor cleavage between Gly22 and Thr23 was observed for all SpA variants.
source: Precursor cleavage between Gly22 and Thr23 was observed for all SpA variants, suggesting that it represents a proteolytic event unrelated to the function of the YSIRK/GXXS motif in targeting SpA secretion to septal membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from Edman degradation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SecA was the most abundant protein that co-purified with SpAED/S18L.
source: SecA was the most abundant protein.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: SecA co-purification with SpAED/S18L, but not SpAED, from staphylococcal extracts was detected by immunoblotting both in the presence and in the absence of crosslinking agent.
source: In agreement with this model, SecA co-purification with SpAED/S18L, but not SpAED, from staphylococcal extracts was detected by immunoblotting both in the presence and in the absence of crosslinking agent (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: SecA did not co-purify with formaldehyde-treated SpAED/SP-SasF.
source: SecA also did not co-purify with formaldehyde-treated SpAED/SP-SasF (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Most of the proteins crosslinked to SpAED/S18L are components of the peptidoglycan, wall teichoic acid and lipoteichoic acid synthesis pathways that are known to be localized to septal membranes.
source: Most of the proteins crosslinked to SpAED/S18L are components of the peptidoglycan (PBP2, MurE2, MurG, FemA, FemB, FemX), wall teichoic acid (TagB, TagF) and lipoteichoic acid synthesis pathways (LtaS) that are known to be localized to septal membranes (Pinho and Errington, 2005; Mann et al., 2013; Reichmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1 and citations to prior work on protein localization.

claim: S. aureus mutants lacking EzrA, PBP2, PurL, ClpB, ClpC, PknB, SAOUHSC_01854, SAOUHSC_02423, or SAOUHSC_01583 did not exhibit defects in septal precursor translocation.
source: When analyzed for SpA trafficking via immunofluorescence microscopy, S. aureus mutants lacking EzrA, PBP2, PurL, ClpB, ClpC, PknB, SAOUHSC_01854, SAOUHSC_02423 (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine pyrophosphorylase), or SAOUHSC_01583 (conserved hypothetical phage protein) did not exhibit defects in septal precursor translocation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In E. coli, secA is an essential gene.
source: In Escherichia coli, secA is an essential gene (Oliver and Beckwith, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: When induced with IPTG, S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) forms colonies on agar and replicates in liquid media culture in a manner similar to wild-type S. aureus.
source: When induced with isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactoside (IPTG), S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) forms colonies on agar and replicates in liquid media culture in a manner similar to wild-type S. aureus (Figure 5bc).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve and colony formation data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: Following dilution of bacteria from IPTG-containing media into broth without inducer, S. aureus WY223 replicates for 3 hr at a rate similar to wild-type.
source: Following dilution of bacteria from IPTG-containing media into broth without inducer, S. aureus WY223 replicates for 3 hr at a rate similar to wild-type (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Upon further dilution and incubation, S. aureus WY223 eventually exhibits growth retardation (6 hr time point).
source: Upon further dilution and incubation, S. aureus WY223 eventually exhibits growth retardation (6 hr time point).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: SecA was already depleted in S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) cultures 3 hr following dilution into inducer free medium.
source: When analyzed by immunoblotting with SecA-specific antibody, SecA was already depleted in S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) cultures 3 hr following dilution into inducer free medium (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: After 6 hr of incubation, SecA could no longer be detected.
source: After 6 hr of incubation, SecA could no longer be detected (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Depletion of SecA does not cause immediate growth retardation in S. aureus WY223.
source: These observations indicate that depletion of SecA does not cause immediate growth retardation in S. aureus WY223; SecA-depletion likely impairs replenishment of translocated proteins that are required for staphylococcal growth, which manifests after 6 hr of SecA depletion.
evidence: This is inferred from growth and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In wild-type, SpA precursors are processed within 60 s.
source: In wild-type, SpA precursors are processed within 60 s; similar rates of processing were observed when the Pspac-secA mutant was grown with IPTG inducer (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In the absence of IPTG, SpA precursor processing was slowed to about 5 min in the Pspac-secA mutant.
source: In the absence of IPTG, SpA precursor processing was slowed to about 5 min, indicating that SecA depletion inhibits precursor translocation (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Wild-type S. aureus deposited protein A into the cross wall.
source: When analyzed by fluorescence microcopy in trypsin-treated staphylococci incubated for 20 min without protease, wild-type S. aureus deposited protein A into the cross wall (Figure 6b, yellow arrow).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Cross wall localization was diminished in Pspac-secA mutant bacteria grown without IPTG inducer.
source: Cross wall localization was diminished in Pspac-secA mutant bacteria grown without IPTG inducer and restored to wild-type levels when bacteria were grown in the presence of inducer (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: Six hours after dilution into broth without IPTG inducer, S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) cells were grossly enlarged and surrounded by a thin layer of peptidoglycan with aberrant cross-wall formation.
source: Six hours after dilution into broth without IPTG inducer, S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) cells were grossly enlarged and surrounded by a thin layer of peptidoglycan with aberrant cross-wall formation (Figure 6d, blue arrow); at this time point, SpA could not be detected in the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Depletion of SecA in S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) caused a reduction in secreted Geh.
source: When analyzed by immunoblotting of proteins in the extracellular medium, depletion of SecA in S. aureus WY223 (Pspac-secA) caused a reduction in secreted Geh, as compared to wild-type staphylococci or S. aureus WY223 grown in the presence of IPTG (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The abundance of secreted Nuc was diminished in SecA-depleted cultures of S. aureus WY223.
source: The abundance of secreted Nuc was also diminished in SecA-depleted cultures of S. aureus WY223 (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Production of sortase A in staphylococcal membranes was not affected by the depletion of SecA.
source: As a control, production of sortase A in staphylococcal membranes was not affected by the depletion of SecA.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: SecA is essential for S. aureus growth.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that SecA is essential for S. aureus growth and for the secretion of precursors with canonical and YSIRK/GXXS signal peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from growth and secretion data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: SecA is essential for the secretion of precursors with canonical and YSIRK/GXXS signal peptides.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that SecA is essential for S. aureus growth and for the secretion of precursors with canonical and YSIRK/GXXS signal peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from secretion data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of secA:sfGFP in the Pspac-secA variant restored bacterial growth in the absence of IPTG inducer.
source: Expression of secA:sfGFP in the Pspac-secA variant restored bacterial growth in the absence of IPTG inducer, indicating that secA-gfp is functional (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: secA:sfGFP is functional.
source: Expression of secA:sfGFP in the Pspac-secA variant restored bacterial growth in the absence of IPTG inducer, indicating that secA-gfp is functional (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is inferred from growth restoration data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Growth restoration occurred in the presence and in the absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc).
source: Growth restoration occurred in the presence and in the absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc), suggesting that secA:sfGFP must be expressed even in the absence of the Ptet inducer (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: S. aureus WY230 produced small amounts SecA:sfGFP in the absence of ATc.
source: Immunoblotting of staphylococcal cell extracts 3 and 6 hr following dilution into media lacking IPTG revealed that S. aureus WY230 indeed produced small amounts SecA:sfGFP in the absence of ATc (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: In the presence of ATc inducer, the abundance of SecA-GFP was increased.
source: In the presence of ATc inducer, the abundance of SecA-GFP was increased (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Under SecA depleting conditions, even small amounts of SecA-sfGFP in S. aureus WY230 (-ATc) restored precursor processing of pulse-labeled SpA.
source: However, under SecA depleting conditions, even small amounts of SecA-sfGFP in S. aureus WY230 (-ATc) restored precursor processing of pulse-labeled SpA (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: SpA precursor processing was accelerated to levels faster than wild-type when S. aureus WY230 cultures were grown in the presence of ATc.
source: SpA precursor processing was accelerated to levels faster than wild-type when S. aureus WY230 cultures were grown in the presence of ATc (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: SecA-sfGFP was found on septal and on polar membranes in dividing cells.
source: In dividing cells, SecA-sfGFP was found on septal and on polar membranes (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: ATc-induced overexpression of SecA-sfGFP caused accumulation of hybrid protein throughout plasma membranes.
source: ATc-induced overexpression of SecA-sfGFP caused accumulation of hybrid protein throughout plasma membranes (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: In S. aureus WY230, SecA-sfGFP is associated with all membranes and is not restricted to septal membranes.
source: Thus, in S. aureus WY230, SecA-sfGFP is associated with all membranes and is not restricted to septal membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: In S. aureus WY223 producing wild-type levels of SecA (Pspac-secA +IPTG), SpA precursors were localized to septal membranes.
source: In S. aureus WY223 producing wild-type levels of SecA (Pspac-secA +IPTG), SpA precursors were localized to septal membranes (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: SpA precursors appeared as two puncta or ring deposits at septal membranes.
source: In other images, SpA precursors appeared as two puncta or ring deposits at septal membranes, reminiscent of FtsZ and of the division rings that are known to accumulate at this site (Figure 8ab) (Lutkenhaus, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8a and 8b.

claim: Under SecA depleting conditions (-IPTG), SpA precursors in S. aureus WY223 were associated with polar membranes and were not localized to septal membranes.
source: In contrast, under SecA depleting conditions (-IPTG), SpA precursors in S. aureus WY223 were associated with polar membranes and were not localized to septal membranes (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The secDF gene is not essential for protein secretion and S. aureus growth.
source: The secDF gene is not essential for protein secretion and S. aureus growth, however secDF mutants exhibit diminished secretion of many precursors secreted via canonical and YSIRK-GXXS signal peptides (Quiblier et al., 2011; Quiblier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: secDF mutants exhibit diminished secretion of many precursors secreted via canonical and YSIRK-GXXS signal peptides.
source: The secDF gene is not essential for protein secretion and S. aureus growth, however secDF mutants exhibit diminished secretion of many precursors secreted via canonical and YSIRK-GXXS signal peptides (Quiblier et al., 2011; Quiblier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Compared to wild-type S. aureus, the ΔsecDF mutant accumulated SpAED precursor in bacterial cells and secreted reduced amounts of mature SpAED into the extracellular medium.
source: Compared to wild-type S. aureus, the ΔsecDF mutant (S. aureus WY418) accumulated SpAED precursor in bacterial cells and secreted reduced amounts of mature SpAED into the extracellular medium (Figure 9ab).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: S. aureus rnd2 (WY416) and rnd3 (WY400) mutants exhibited wild-type levels of SpAED secretion.
source: S. aureus rnd2 (WY416) and rnd3 (WY400) mutants exhibited wild-type levels of SpAED secretion (Figure 9ab).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: A variant (WY412) lacking all three genes, ΔsecDF Δrnd23, accumulated precursors at a level similar to the ΔsecDF mutant.
source: A variant (WY412) lacking all three genes, ΔsecDF Δrnd23, accumulated precursors at a level similar to the ΔsecDF mutant (Figure 9ab).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: The ΔsecDF mutant secreted diminished amounts of Geh and failed to secrete Coa.
source: When analyzed for other secreted proteins, the ΔsecDF mutant secreted diminished amounts of Geh and failed to secrete Coa, whose precursor is secreted via a canonical signal peptide (Phonimdaeng et al., 1990), while the Δrnd2 and Δrnd3 variants displayed wild-type phenotypes (Figure 9ab).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: SecDF, but not Rnd2 and Rnd3, contributes to protein secretion in S. aureus.
source: Thus, SecDF, but not Rnd2 and Rnd3, contributes to protein secretion in S. aureus.
evidence: This is inferred from immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9a and 9b.

claim: Septal secretion of SpA was diminished in the ∆secDF and ΔsecDF Δrnd23 mutants.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy experiments revealed that septal secretion of SpA was diminished in the ∆secDF and ΔsecDF Δrnd23 mutants (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: ∆secDF and ΔsecDF Δrnd23 mutants exhibited puncta of SpA precursors and rings of low fluorescent intensity at septal membranes.
source: Unlike SecA-depleted cells, where SpA precursors failed to associate with septal membranes, ∆secDF and ΔsecDF Δrnd23 mutants exhibited puncta of SpA precursors and rings of low fluorescent intensity at septal membranes (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: The diminished abundance of SpA precursors at septal membranes was restored to wild-type levels by plasmid-borne expression of secDF in ∆secDF (pSecDF) and in ΔsecDF Δrnd23 (pSecDF) staphylococci.
source: The diminished abundance of SpA precursors at septal membranes was restored to wild-type levels by plasmid-borne expression of secDF in ∆secDF (pSecDF) and in ΔsecDF Δrnd23 (pSecDF) staphylococci (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: SecDF aids in the translocation of SpA across staphylococcal membranes but is not absolutely required for precursor targeting to septal membranes.
source: These data suggest that SecDF aids in the translocation of SpA across staphylococcal membranes but is not absolutely required for precursor targeting to septal membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: LtaS-mediated synthesis of lipoteichoic acid is essential for S. aureus growth and cell division.
source: LtaS-mediated synthesis of lipoteichoic acid, a polyglycerol-phosphate polymer decorated with esterified D-alanyl and GlcNAc residues, is essential for S. aureus growth and cell division (Gründling and Schneewind, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LtaS depletion (-IPTG) resulted in SpA deposition into polar peptidoglycan.
source: LtaS depletion (-IPTG) resulted in SpA deposition into polar peptidoglycan, whereas under LtaS inducing conditions (+IPTG) SpA was localized in the cross-wall (Figure 10bc).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 10b and quantification in Figure 10c.

claim: Under LtaS inducing conditions (+IPTG) SpA was localized in the cross-wall.
source: LtaS depletion (-IPTG) resulted in SpA deposition into polar peptidoglycan, whereas under LtaS inducing conditions (+IPTG) SpA was localized in the cross-wall (Figure 10bc).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 10b and quantification in Figure 10c.

claim: Without IPTG inducer, S. aureus ANG499 mislocalized SpA precursors to polar membranes.
source: In contrast, without IPTG inducer, S. aureus ANG499 mislocalized SpA precursors to polar membranes (Figure 10d).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 10d.

claim: LtaS depletion in S. aureus ANG499 (Pspac-ltaS, -IPTG) diminished the abundance of cell wall anchored SpA without affecting the secretion of Geh and Nuc.
source: These experiments revealed that LtaS depletion in S. aureus ANG499 (Pspac-ltaS, -IPTG) diminished the abundance of cell wall anchored SpA without affecting the secretion of Geh and Nuc (Figure 10e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 10e.

claim: LtaS depletion diminished the overall surface distribution of SpA.
source: Consistent with the immunoblotting results, LtaS depletion diminished the overall surface distribution of SpA (Figure 10f), in agreement with the hypothesis that cross-wall targeting via the YSIRK/GXXS signal peptide, but not polar secretion, is responsible for efficient surface distribution of proteins in staphylococci (Carlsson et al., 2006; DeDent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 10f.

claim: LtaS depletion and a block in lipoteichoic acid synthesis abolished SpA precursor trafficking to septal membranes without affecting its secretion at polar membranes.
source: Together these data indicate that LtaS depletion and a block in lipoteichoic acid synthesis abolished SpA precursor trafficking to septal membranes without affecting its secretion at polar membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from fluorescence microscopy and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Cell wall-anchored surface proteins with YSIRK/GXXS motif signal peptides have been identified in streptococcal and staphylococcal species.
source: Cell wall-anchored surface proteins with YSIRK/GXXS motif signal peptides have been identified in streptococcal and staphylococcal species (Tettelin et al., 2005; Rosenstein and Götz, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The signal peptides of surface proteins in the genus Actinomyces, Bacillus, Clostridium, and Listeria do not contain the YSIRK/GXXS motif.
source: Although sortase-anchored surface proteins are found in many different gram-positive bacteria, the signal peptides of surface proteins in the genus Actinomyces, Bacillus, Clostridium, and Listeria do not contain the YSIRK/GXXS motif.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about signal peptide sequences in different bacterial genera.

claim: Common features of staphylococci and streptococci are their spherical or ovoid cell shapes and cell wall synthesis programs at septal membranes.
source: Common features of staphylococci and streptococci are their spherical or ovoid cell shapes and cell wall synthesis programs at septal membranes; in staphylococci this compartment is designated as the cross-wall (Giesbrecht et al., 1976; Touhami et al., 2004; Monteiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The YSIRK/GXXS motif of the SpA precursor is dispensable for sortase-catalyzed cell wall anchoring.
source: Earlier work demonstrated that the YSIRK/GXXS motif of the SpA precursor is dispensable for sortase-catalyzed cell wall anchoring (Bae and Schneewind, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: YSIRK/GXXS motif cleavage may represent a mechanism for precursor translocation at septal membranes.
source: On the basis of these observations, we are compelled to speculate that YSIRK/GXXS motif cleavage may represent a mechanism for precursor translocation at septal membranes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed cleavage patterns.

claim: The YSIRK/GXXS motif may inhibit a key function of the adjacent hydrophobic core within signal peptides: promoting the membrane translocation of precursors.
source: For example, the YSIRK/GXXS motif may inhibit a key function of the adjacent hydrophobic core within signal peptides: promoting the membrane translocation of precursors.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of YSIRK/GXXS function.

claim: Such inhibitory mechanism could be relieved by a YSIRK/GXXS protease that localizes to the septal membrane.
source: Such inhibitory mechanism could be relieved by a YSIRK/GXXS protease that localizes to the septal membrane.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about a potential protease mechanism.

claim: SecA appears to bind directly to the signal peptide of SpAED/S18L.
source: SecA appears to bind directly to the signal peptide of SpAED/S18L.
evidence: This is inferred from co-purification data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The resulting complex may even engage SecYEG translocase as well as SecDF.
source: The resulting complex may even engage SecYEG translocase as well as SecDF.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known interactions of SecA with SecYEG.

claim: It seems unlikely that LtaS may directly interact with SpAED/S18L.
source: It seems unlikely that LtaS may directly interact with SpAED/S18L.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the crosslinking data.

claim: SpAED/S18L complexed with SecA and SecYEG at septal membranes can be crosslinked to other septal proteins.
source: We think it is plausible that SpAED/S18L complexed with SecA and SecYEG at septal membranes can be crosslinked to other septal proteins.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the crosslinking results.

claim: S. aureus SecA is localized to the plasma membrane and is not spatially restricted to septal membranes or microdomains.
source: We show here that S. aureus SecA is localized to the plasma membrane and is not spatially restricted to septal membranes or microdomains.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: This distribution is consistent with our proposed role of SecA, promoting precursor translocation at polar and septal membranes.
source: This distribution is consistent with our proposed role of SecA, promoting precursor translocation at polar and septal membranes.
evidence: This is inference based on the observed SecA localization.

claim: Septal accumulation of LtaS and of lipoteichoic acids functions as a determinant for SecA-mediated targeting of SpA precursors.
source: We have incorporated these observations into a model whereby septal accumulation of LtaS and of lipoteichoic acids functions as a determinant for SecA-mediated targeting of SpA precursors.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: Following precursor cleavage at the YSIRK/GXXS motif, truncated SpA (SpA-2) is moved across the membrane, aided by the proton-motif force and by the chaperone activity of SecDF.
source: Following precursor cleavage at the YSIRK/GXXS motif, truncated SpA (SpA-2) is moved across the membrane, aided by the proton-motif force and by the chaperone activity of SecDF.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: RseP is not involved in septal secretion and cleavage of the YSIRK-GXXS signal peptides.
source: However, RseP is not involved in septal secretion and cleavage of the YSIRK-GXXS signal peptides, as a deletion of the corresponding gene does not affect SpA septal secretion in the S. aureusΔSAOUHSC_01239 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
